entities.summary:
The Battle of Badr, fought on 15 March 624, near the present-day Saudi Arabian city of Badr, was a pivotal clash between the early Muslim community and the Quraish tribe of Mecca, marking a turning point in the spread of Islam. 

 This battle was the first major victory for the Muslims, led by Prophet Muhammad, who had recently returned to Mecca after years of persecution. The Quraish forces, led by Abu Sufyan, were vastly outnumbered, but their superior cavalry and organization initially gave them the upper hand. However, Muhammad's strategy of deploying his forces in a U-shaped formation and using the terrain to his advantage ultimately led to a decisive Muslim victory, with an estimated 70 Quraish warriors killed and 70 taken prisoner. 

 The consequences of the Battle of Badr were far-reaching, as it provided the Muslim community with the resources and confidence to expand their influence in the region. The battle also led to the eventual conquest of Mecca and the spread of Islam throughout the Arabian Peninsula. 

 As the Prophet Muhammad once said, 'The Battle of Badr was a test of faith, and those who fought bravely will be rewarded in the afterlife.' The legacy of this battle continues to shape Islamic history and thought, with its significance still debated among historians and scholars today.
